This is undeniable, and it has nothing to do with “idealism.”
Idealism claims that my knowledge “creates” things and that without me they would cease to exist.
In reality, all we can say is that the things I actually know do not, as a matter of fact, exist without my knowledge of them—although they obviously could exist without it.

My desk includes both the weight of my hand resting on it and my knowledge of the desk. If we “abstract away” either that weight or that knowledge, we turn the concrete table before us into an “abstract” desk.

53) It has long been recognized that the so-called “secondary” qualities—color and appearance, for example, as opposed to weight and shape—do not exist apart from human beings, or more generally apart from living beings equipped with sense organs.
Physics, however, deals with the “primary” qualities, such as space, time, and mass, and so might seem to deal with “things in themselves,” independently of humanity.
Contemporary quantum physics has shown that this is not so.

Heisenberg’s “uncertainty principle,” for example, would make no sense if physics did not take into account the fact that, for physics, only things we can observe exist—that is, things we can observe with our eyes, by means of light.
The electron therefore stands in relation to a human “observer” in exactly the same way as a mountain or the color of a desert does.
Even in geometry, the “observing subject” is represented by a coordinate system.
But this book is hardly the place to discuss all of that.
I will therefore say only that in physics itself, the attempt to “abstract away” the subject leads to obvious physical errors.
Even so, contemporary physics does not become philosophy merely because it includes the subject in its investigations.
The subject it includes is not a concrete human being, but an abstraction—an eye “in general,” or even an idealized eye.
So although physics includes the observer, it still “abstracts away” the fact that the concrete subject not only sees but also always “feels,” “acts,” and so on.
54) All of this will become clearer only later.
For now I will simply note that the conception of the human being as an essentially historical entity, rather than as a thing possessing eternal qualities, was first stated clearly by Hegel.
Marx adopted the same conception, notably when he spoke of the “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom.”

But this conception, like Hegelianism as a whole, had been quietly prepared by Judeo-Christian theological thought, whereas the conception of the human being as a thing goes back to pagan Greek philosophy and science.

A medieval Jewish thinker, for example, could be convinced that the difference between a Jew, a member of the “chosen people,” and a “goy,” a non-Jew, was so great that the two should not even be brought together under the same concept of “human being.”
That opposition between Jew and goy is obviously absurd.

But it is true that the difference between people belonging to different historical worlds can be so great that knowing the qualities they have in common does not amount to knowing what constitutes their specifically human, or historical, essence.
55) We now know that the system of definitions and axioms attributed to “Euclid” does not exhaust all geometrically possible systems of definitions and axioms.
There are also non-Euclidean geometrical “things”—triangles, for example, whose angles add up to more or less than two right angles.

But this does nothing to undermine the truth of Euclidean geometry, because from the outset that geometry seeks to study only those geometrical “things” that satisfy the definitions and axioms laid down by “Euclid.”

It is true that, as the work of Hilbert and others has shown, drawing up the complete list of axioms with no unnecessary elements—and above all proving that the system contains no contradiction—is an extraordinarily difficult task requiring in practice an immense amount of work.
But in principle there is no insurmountable difficulty here.
56) As I have already said, geometrical “axioms” are not in any sense self-evident truths.
When applied to real space, they are only hypotheses, since we are still far from knowing the geometrical structure of our actual space, which is very probably not Euclidean.
Within pure geometry, meanwhile, “axioms” are simply “postulates,” or definitions of the objects to be studied. It therefore makes no sense to ask whether they are true or false.
Lobachevskian geometry, for example, is neither more nor less “true” than “Euclidean” geometry.

The choice of mathematical “axioms” is completely arbitrary. They need only avoid contradicting one another and form a closed system corresponding to a definite group of “things” that exist “mathematically,” or ideally.

In other words, using these “axioms” alone, it must be possible to “construct” every mathematical “thing” belonging to the system, just as a circle, triangle, square, and so on can be constructed using the axioms and definitions of “Euclid.”
57) For many centuries it was regarded as “self-evident” that the whole is greater than its part.
After Cantor, however, we know that this is not always so.
The number of even numbers, for example, is not smaller than the number of all whole numbers, even though the even numbers form only a part of them.
If we write the sequence of whole numbers
and then multiply each number by two, the number of members in the sequence has obviously not changed. Yet we have transformed it into the sequence of even numbers.
There are therefore exactly as many even numbers as there are whole numbers in general, even though the even numbers are certainly only a part of all numbers—and apparently half of them.
58) For Spinoza’s philosophical system to be possible, the philosopher would have to stand in the same position as the geometer: he would have to construct his own object—that is, his own “axioms.”
This is what idealism claims, and in this sense idealism is more logical than realism, including Spinoza’s realism.
An a priori idealist system is certainly possible.
Unfortunately, however, idealism itself is uncertain.

No one can prevent us, of course, from constructing “a priori philosophical systems.” But there would be no way of determining whether such systems were true or false—that is, whether they corresponded to anything that actually exists.
Constructing systems of this kind is merely a game played with concepts, comparable at best to a game of cards or chess.
59) I must emphasize again that none of this will become convincing until the book itself has been read.
60) Marx speaks of dialectical and historical materialism.
But I have already explained the sense in which this should be understood. (See note 27.)
The concept of dialectic will be defined in Section II of the second part of this introduction. (See pp. 311–396.)
The book as a whole is, moreover, an example of Hegelian-Marxist dialectic in practice.
61) Hegel obviously did not think his system in fact contained everything human beings could ever possibly say.
It needed to contain everything only in principle.

Every proposition within the system can therefore be developed more fully than Hegel himself developed it. But that further development will itself be circular and return to its starting point. It cannot therefore destroy the course of the system’s development.
The system is the fundamental circle of knowledge. Every point on that circle can itself be developed into another circle, and every point on those circles can in turn become a circle, and so on.
Taken together in their full development, these systems therefore form a single circle composed of circles, themselves composed of further circles.
Knowledge can consequently continue to develop even after the system has appeared.
But this later development adds nothing fundamentally new, and in any case it does not destroy the system.

If one wishes, one can say that a circular system functions as a complete system of “axioms” embracing knowledge as a whole, just as the system of “Euclid’s” axioms embraces the whole of Euclidean geometry.
Hegel therefore does not break with the philosophical tradition.

He merely discovered how to achieve what his predecessors had unsuccessfully tried to achieve. They had failed to recognize the fundamental difference between a philosophical system of knowledge as such and a system—mathematical, for example—of some limited field of knowledge.
62) We can see that Hegel was mistaken not only because history continued after his system appeared, but also because the circularity of his system is only apparent.
In fact, the “Phenomenology” found near the end of the Encyclopedia does not coincide with the Phenomenology that is supposed to serve as the introduction to the Encyclopedia.
But I cannot go into this question in the present book.
63) I put the adjective “true” in quotation marks because, strictly speaking, only “wisdom”—that is, omniscience—is true.
Philosophy is not, because its knowledge remains only partial.
We can call philosophy true only in the sense that it knows its own imperfection and knows the character of perfect knowledge.
64) Experience shows that reason does not in fact produce one single form of speech but many: human beings speak many different languages.
Yet because every language can be translated into another, we can say that, in principle, there is only one rational, meaningful discourse.
Whether the meaning of the French word cheval is expressed by the Latin equus or the German Pferd, the three words still “mean” or “refer to” the same thing.
In general, the semantic content of discourse remains the same. Only its spoken or written form changes.
Translation is the replacement of one set of linguistic sounds by another.

The unlimited possibility of translating all discourse—or, which amounts to the same thing, of communicating it without limit—shows, and this alone shows, that there is only one reason and that it is always the same, unchanging reason.
We assume, of course, that reason does not exist apart from human beings. Animals exist but have no reason, while angels and god, who are supposedly rational, do not exist.
But this means only the following.

Since there are many human beings, there are also many individual instances of reason and intellect. Yet reason is wholly present in every human being, because every human being can understand any discourse.
There is therefore no difference in principle between the reason of one individual and that of another, since all discourse is communicable without limit.
65) Suppose someone says to me: “a round square.”
I have no difficulty understanding what is being said. I know that we are talking about a square rather than something else, and that it is being described as round rather than in some other way.
The expression is therefore fully meaningful and communicable.
But the moment I try to combine the meanings of the words “a,” “square,” and “round,” taken separately, I discover that I cannot form a single overall meaning from the three of them.
Discourses of this kind are called incoherent or contradictory.

(In the narrow sense, “incoherent” is sometimes used for sentences such as: “in vain the house from the fact of swimming red.” Strictly speaking, however, such strings are simply meaningless, even though they are articulated and made up of meaningful words.
I therefore include “coherence” in this narrow sense within the broader idea of “meaningfulness” or “communicability,” and reserve the word “incoherent” for contradictory discourse.)
“A herring wants to swim. And man laughs. When it flies, It dies at once.”
The statement is articulated, meaningful, and coherent. But it is neither convincing nor demonstrable.
No one will accept it as truth.
Understanding it therefore gives us no knowledge, and there is no necessity compelling us to accept its meaning or affirm it.
